prize_parts.citation: for foundational contributions to the theory of nominal rigidities and monetary policy: time-dependent price setting, staggered contracts and interest-rate rules, and the micro-founded, welfare-based theory of interest and prices

statement.case_for: My configuration does not change: B014 with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. What changed is how I would defend it, in response to the chair's questions and the round-1 exchange. The case rests on three separable, load-bearing conceptual steps. Calvo supplied the tractable pricing friction that makes a forward-looking Phillips curve possible. Taylor supplied staggered contracts and the policy rule that disciplined thinking about systematic policy. Woodford integrated them into a welfare-based general-equilibrium theory of interest and prices. The work is 25 to 40 years old and was tested through 2008, the zero lower bound and the post-2020 inflation. On the chair's question about the post-2021 evidence, I read it as extension, not as grounds for doubting maturity. The most informative observation from my own field is that heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian models keep Calvo-type nominal rigidity and an interest-rate rule as their nominal block and change the household and demand side. A superseded framework would not be kept as the base layer of its critics' models. This is my reading from background knowledge, not an independently verified claim. Against B003, my ordering rests on two criteria stated without reference to support counts: breadth of influence on how the field analyses and conducts policy, and marginal distinctiveness given earlier prizes. On both, I still place the nominal-rigidity and rule core ahead of collateral-constraint amplification, although Kiyotaki-Moore is the cleaner attribution and is a defensible fallback.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the main weakness. Galí, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, Gertler, Smets and Wouters have major claims, and a three-person cap excludes the estimated-DSGE strand that made the framework usable in central banks. Swapping Galí for Calvo does not fix this, because Galí's strongest claim is development and empirical grounding of the Calvo structure. A citation weighted toward the empirical tradition would need Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans or Smets and Wouters, which the cap does not allow. Calvo's contribution is also compact, and Fredriksson reasonably asks whether it is a discovery in the sense the committee normally rewards. Finally, representative-agent versions are widely seen as superseded, so the prize could be read as rewarding a stage of development, and the committee has not settled whether earlier macro prizes (rational expectations, time consistency, VAR methods, banking crises) leave enough marginal room.

responses.point: Strömberg accepts B014's policy importance but says the citation must say whether it rewards the pricing friction, the policy rule or the integrated framework, since these are different discoveries. He would support B014 given a defensible narrower citation, and otherwise considers B003 the cleaner prize.
responses.response: I think the citation can meet this condition by naming the three components and tying each to one laureate. It would credit a joint contribution to the nominal-rigidity and policy-rule core of monetary analysis, not the whole New Keynesian literature, and it should say nothing about estimation or the medium-scale DSGE tradition. That still leaves Galí, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, Smets and Gertler outside it, and I would not claim the wording removes that cost. I agree B003 is the cleaner attribution and, as my first alternative, a defensible choice. I rank B014 higher on breadth of influence on practice and because the 2022 prize narrows B003's marginal room, though your point that collateral borrowing constraints differ from intermediation and bank runs is fair and weakens that last argument.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson keeps Calvo over Galí because Calvo's pricing mechanism is the primitive of the New Keynesian Phillips curve. She would not object strongly to Galí in Calvo's place if the committee weights empirical validation and the estimated-model tradition more heavily.
responses.response: I agree on the structure of the contributions. I would add that the swap does not do what a more empirical citation needs. Galí's contribution is the Phillips curve and policy analysis built on Calvo pricing. The identification and estimation strand that made the framework usable belongs to Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans and to Smets and Wouters. If the committee wants a citation weighted toward estimated models, changing the third name would be insufficient. It would need a different trio, and I would then ask whether that is still the same achievement. I therefore keep the conceptual-foundations citation and Calvo. If the committee prefers Galí, I would not treat it as a disqualifying difference.

responses.point: Andersson moved to Calvo, Taylor and Woodford but maintains that the Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans contribution on identifying monetary shocks and estimating a medium-scale model is not derivative, and that a citation limited to mechanisms and rules does not capture it.
responses.response: I agree, and that is why I would not describe the omission as minor or as implied by lower merit. Identifying monetary shocks and estimating a medium-scale model is a different kind of contribution from the mechanisms, and it deserves its own credit. A citation limited to pricing friction, contracts and rule, and welfare-based synthesis should say that and no more. The cap makes the cost real. I do not think it makes the attribution unresolvable, because the three credited contributions are separable and each is identifiable in specific bodies of work.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B047 first for its clean two-name attribution, ranks B014 second, and argues that Calvo's and Taylor's older contract-pricing insights differ from the Woodford and Galí synthesis, so the committee must say which it is crediting.
responses.response: Clean attribution counts in B047's favour, and I do not deny it. I weigh it less than you do because of the Krugman 2008 overlap and the unresolved priority of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum. On your point about layers, I think the committee can credit the line from origin to synthesis. The pricing friction and the contract-and-rule idea are the primitives, and Woodford's synthesis is the step that turned them into a policy-evaluation theory. That is one lineage, not a mixture of generations. I should also say again, as you did, that we are frequent co-authors, so readers should weigh my agreement or disagreement with you accordingly.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B003 first with the Kiyotaki-Moore pair and treats the 2022 overlap as a citation-drafting matter, namely naming the collateral-constraint mechanism specifically. He keeps B014 as his first alternative, and his hesitation is attribution.
responses.response: I accept that a citation naming the collateral-constraint mechanism separates it from bank runs and intermediation more than I allowed in round 1, so I weigh the overlap less than I did. I still see a modest difference in marginal room, and I do not think drafting removes it. On attribution, I agree B003 is cleaner. The question is whether cleaner credit should outweigh the larger reach of the other work. I think not, but I regard the two as a close comparison and would support B003 if the committee judged B014's attribution problem unsolvable.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a citation limited to pricing friction, contracts and rule, and welfare-based synthesis, and whether it reads that wording as an implicit ranking against Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, Smets, Wouters, Galí and Gertler.
Whether Calvo or Galí is the better third name. I judge Calvo's pricing device to be the primitive, but a committee that weights the empirical framework more could reasonably decide otherwise.

How much weight the post-2021 inflation episode and the heterogeneous-agent critique should carry. I read heterogeneous-agent models that keep Calvo pricing and a policy rule as evidence of foundational status, but I am in that field, and others could read the same evidence as grounds for caution.
How much marginal room the 2022 prize leaves for B003, and how much the 2008 trade prize and the 2024 institutions prize should count against B047 and B032.
My priority and attribution judgements rest on background knowledge of the literature and were not independently verified from the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. My supplied profile lists no co-authorship with Calvo, Taylor or Woodford. My field is macroeconomic theory, including heterogeneous-agent models that extend or criticise the B014 framework, and I record that as field proximity and possible bias. My listed long-term co-authors include committee members Hassler (chair, a B014 supporter) and Boppart (B047 supporter), who are not candidates, and Boppart has also disclosed our frequent co-authorship. I have tried not to treat agreement with Hassler as evidence of merit. For the alternatives, B003 has no apparent connection to me. For B032, my institution, the IIES in Stockholm, is associated with political economics and my profile does not state Persson's affiliation, so a possible institutional connection should be noted. Teorell has disclosed co-authorship with Persson. Conflicts are disclosed and not adjudicated.
